analysis.one_liner: Repeals corporate and estate taxes, taxes only wages at 10%, and forgives all prior income taxes.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing, vote, or cosponsor: it died in the Ways and Means Committee.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would abolish the corporate income tax, the estate tax, and the gift tax, replace all individual income tax rates with a flat 10 percent tax on wages and self-employment earnings only, and wipe out every deduction, credit, and exclusion. It would also forgive all federal income taxes owed for years before 2000, including any unpaid back taxes. Capital gains, dividends, and other investment income would not be taxed at all.
analysis.who_benefits: Wealthy households and profitable corporations. Corporations would owe no income tax ever again. People with investment income (capital gains, dividends, interest, rents, pensions) would owe nothing on it, so the tax burden on wealth would go to zero while everyone still earning a paycheck would pay 10 percent. Anyone with unpaid taxes from before 2000, including tax evaders, would be off the hook. Large estates would no longer face the estate tax.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the corporate income tax entirely, so corporations would pay no federal income tax on their profits.
Taxes only wages and self-employment earnings at 10 percent; dividends, capital gains, interest, rents, pensions, and annuities would be untaxed.
Repeals all estate, gift, and generation-skipping taxes.
Forgives all individual income tax liability (with penalties and interest) for tax years before 2000, except amounts already paid and taxes attributable to illegal activities.

analysis.who_pays: Everyone who earns a paycheck or self-employment income. After losing the corporate tax, the estate and gift taxes, and taxes on investment income, the government's individual income tax revenue would come only from a 10 percent levy on work. Unless replaced by another tax (the bill proposes none), wage earners would bear the full cost of funding the federal government, and programs would face massive cuts.

drawbacks.text: The tax burden would fall almost entirely on income from work, while income from wealth (capital gains, dividends, interest, rents) would go untaxed; the only tax on corporate profits would leak through as wages.
The tax amnesty would forgive all back income taxes owed for years before 2000, meaning people who had never filed or paid would owe nothing.

Eliminating the corporate tax, estate tax, and most individual income tax revenue would leave a massive budget gap the bill does not fill, forcing either deep cuts to federal programs or large new borrowing.
Repealing all deductions and credits (including the child tax credit, EITC, and others) would raise taxes on many low- and middle-income households relative to current law, even at a 10 percent rate.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a dramatic shift of the tax burden away from wealth and corporations and onto wages. A 10 percent flat rate on work sounds low, but it would apply with no deductions or credits (no child credit, no EITC), and nothing would tax investment income. The amnesty for pre-2000 taxes would reward nonpayment. The lost revenue (corporate tax, estate tax, taxes on investment income) would have to come from somewhere, likely through deep spending cuts or higher future taxes on whatever income remains taxable: wages. For anyone living on a paycheck, the bill offers a lower rate but a tax code that asks nothing of wealth.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, which never took it up; it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Philip Crane (R-IL) introduced the bill in the House on June 26, 2001.
It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, where it received no further action.
No other member cosponsored the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Corporations and wealthy households would have been the big winners if it had passed, but since it never moved, the existing tax structure remained in place and no one gained from it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one; the bill went nowhere

for.name: Philip M. Crane
for.role: Sponsor, House Ways and Means Committee member

sides.party_line_note: The bill never got a vote and had no cosponsors, so there is no roll-call record of support or opposition.

industries.note: The bill would eliminate the corporate income tax entirely, so corporate profits would go untaxed at the corporate level. The revenue loss would have to be made up by taxing wages or cutting spending.
Repealing the estate, gift, and taxes on investment income, plus the amnesty on back taxes, would substantially reduce the tax burden on the wealthiest households relative to current law.
